mappings.note: Defines an empire against a kingdom through its army, central administration, tax collection across territories and infrastructure - administrative and military machinery. Not CG-SST2, because the specific outcome on how states were run applies.

The factors turning kingdoms into empires - military strength, resource control, taxation, strategy - are the measures a state adopts to expand and hold territory. Not LO-79, because no two rulers are compared.

Alexander's significance is argued through the scale of his empire and the spread of Greek culture into India - a broad historical development. Not LO-78, since no administrative or military measure is analysed.

The Mauryan claim to importance rests on unification, a strong administrative system on Kautilyan lines, infrastructure and governance. Administration carries the answer, so LO-78 rather than the general goal.
Kautilya's saptanga, law and order, economic management and subject welfare are principles of statecraft. Not CG-SST2, because the content is explicitly about how to administer a kingdom.
What was unusual about Ashoka - the turn from conquest to rule by dharma after Kalinga - is the policy of one ruler. Not LO-79, which is kept for items setting two rulers or two systems side by side.

The edict shows officers of dhamma assigned to Buddhists, brahmans, Ajivikas and Jains alike - a measure of imperial administration towards all sects. Not LO-81, because no new religious movement's origin is analysed; the question is about state policy.
A project on the Brahmi script, the writing system through which this period is known. Squarely the 'types of sources' clause of the goal.
Planning a 3rd-century BCE journey down the Dakshinapatha by caravan - travel and trade-route history. No LO in this frame covers commerce or communication.

'Imperium' as supreme power defines the authority an emperor exercises over subject territories - the nature of imperial rule. Not CG-SST2, because the term is about how power is held, which LO-78 addresses.
Samraj and rajadhiraja as titles for a king of kings express supremacy over tributary rulers - the structure of imperial authority. Same treatment as the 'imperium' item.
A tributary kingdom paying tribute as a sign of submission is a device of imperial control. Not CG-SST2, since the item is about the mechanics of holding an empire.
Officials managing territories, collecting taxes and keeping order is the administration outcome stated almost verbatim.
Expansion to gain resources and build economic and military strength is a strategy of state-building. Not CG-SST2, because the reasoning is about power rather than chronology.
Shrenis as guilds of traders and craftsmen is economic and social history. Not LO-68, which is about visiting local markets today under the civics-and-economy goal.
Magadha as the mahajanapada from which the first empire grew - a chronological and geographical fact. Not LO-78, because no administrative measure is named.
Fertile plains, iron ore and navigable rivers behind Magadha's rise is economic geography. Not LO-78, since resources here explain growth rather than describing governance.
Mahapadma Nanda as founder of the Nanda dynasty - dynastic recall. Not LO-78, because unification is stated as a fact, not analysed as a strategy.
Dating Panini and the Ashtadhyayi to the Nanda period. Chronology and textual history under the goal.
Alexander's ambition to reach the 'end of the world' is a motive, not a military measure. Not LO-78, which covers the means of control rather than a conqueror's reasons.

Satraps as provincial governors administering territory for an emperor is a device of imperial administration, and the item invites comparison with Mauryan provinces. Not CG-SST2, because the specific outcome fits.
Porus as the king who fought Alexander in Punjab - a person-and-event recall. Not LO-78, because no strategy is examined, only who resisted.
The hardship and losses of Alexander's return march is narrative history. Not LO-78, since no measure of military control is at issue.
Matches Kautilya, Megasthenes, Panini and Ashoka to their works - identifying the texts through which this period is known, which is the goal's sources clause.
Alexander and the Gymnosophists read as an encounter between Greek and Indian philosophical traditions. Not LO-81: no new religious movement arises from it, and the item is about cultural exchange.
Chandragupta Maurya as founder of the empire in 321 BCE - dynastic chronology. Not LO-78, because how he governed is not asked.

Embankments, village welfare and the idea that royal power rests on a prosperous countryside has to be traced to Kautilya - statecraft and public works. Not CG-SST2, since the content is a governing philosophy.
'Kosha' as the treasury within the saptanga is one of the seven limbs a state is administered through. Administration, so LO-78.
Megasthenes' Indika as the Greek account of Mauryan India - a source historians use. Not LO-78, because the item asks about the book, not the court it describes.

Attributes Ashoka's turn to non-violence to the Buddha's teachings, so the item tests the reach of a new religious movement. Not LO-78, which is used for the administrative side of his dhamma - the officers, edicts and welfare works.

An edict as an official royal command inscribed for subjects is an instrument of administration and communication. Not CG-SST2: although edicts are also sources, the question defines the royal order itself.
'Devanampiya' as a royal title projecting a benevolent ruler belongs with the imperial-authority items. Not LO-81, because the title is political self-presentation rather than religious doctrine.
Ashoka abandoning conquest for dharma-vijaya after Kalinga is a change in a ruler's policy of expansion. Not LO-79, since no other ruler is set against him.

The false statement is that the edicts were in Sanskrit, when they were in Prakrit in Brahmi and other scripts - a point about the sources themselves. Not LO-78, because the key turns on language and script rather than on policy.

Corrects the dating of the Mauryan founding relative to Alexander while accepting that weak successors let the empire fall apart - chronology and the arc of a period. Not LO-78, because no administrative measure is analysed.

The keyed statements are that agriculture was the empire's main revenue and that the Sohagaura inscription shows state food security - fiscal and welfare administration. Not CG-SST2, because revenue and state provision are administrative.
Polished monolithic pillars with animal capitals as Mauryan art. Not LO-80, whose scope is the style and technology of temples, tombs and mosques, none of which a free-standing pillar is.
Dhamma as the moral code Ashoka promoted through his rule is the ideology of his administration. Not LO-81, which is reserved here for the emergence and influence of Buddhism as a movement.

Granaries recorded in the Sohagaura plate show the Mauryan state providing against famine - an administrative measure. Not CG-SST2, even though an inscription is the evidence, because the question asks what it reveals about administration.
The Lion Capital becoming India's national emblem is the afterlife of a historical artefact. Not LO-78, since no aspect of Mauryan governance is involved.
